content:
The Southern Water Tribe appeared first as a line of blue against white.

Katara saw it before I did.

She had been standing near Appa’s head for the last hour, one hand resting against his saddle, eyes fixed on the horizon with a stillness I had learned not to interrupt.

Then her breath changed.

“There.”

Aang moved beside her.

Toph, wrapped in enough fur to qualify as architecture, muttered, “Describe.”

I leaned over the saddle edge.

“Buildings. More than I expected. Blue roofs. Ice walls. Ships in the bay.”

Katara smiled.

It was not uncomplicated.

I could see that too.

She had told me stories of a village small enough that everyone knew who had sneezed before breakfast. Snow huts. A few tents. Children running between them. Her grandmother’s voice. Sokka trying to train six-year-olds as soldiers because all the adults had gone to war.

Below us was a city.

Not Cranefish Town large.

But transformed.

Stone foundations. Timber halls. Water channels. Northern-style towers beside older southern structures. Work crews extending a harbor wall while ships unloaded lumber and grain.

Katara’s home had survived.

Survival had changed it.

Appa landed outside the main settlement in a storm of snow.

Sokka reached us before the snow settled.

He hit Aang first with a hug disguised as a tackle.

Then Katara.

Then Toph, who bent a ridge of ice-crusted earth under his feet and made him stumble.

“Missed you too, Snoozles.”

Sokka looked at me.

“Administrative Companion.”

I stared.

Toph betrayed me with immediate laughter.

“You told him?”

“I wrote him.”

“Why?”

“History.”

Sokka held out both arms.

I stepped into the hug.

“Welcome south,” he said. “We have snow, fish, political arguments, and several buildings my sister has opinions about.”

Katara glared.

“I just got here.”

“You had opinions from the sky.”

“I did not.”

“You made the face.”

Toph pointed at him. “See? Other people can hear faces.”

Gran Gran was waiting at the family home.

Age had made her smaller than I expected and somehow no less formidable. She hugged Katara for a long time, held Aang’s face between both hands, slapped Sokka lightly for hovering, and greeted Toph by saying, “Still barefoot?”

Toph looked delighted.

Then Gran Gran turned toward me.

There are moments when being the newest person in a family feels like standing in a doorway while everyone decides whether it opens.

Gran Gran looked me up and down.

Not assessing my body.

Assessing my nerves.

Then she said, “You’re the one who works with papers.”

Toph made a strangled noise.

I closed my eyes.

“I’m going home.”

Gran Gran laughed and pulled me into a hug.

The door opened.

Dinner lasted three hours.

Hakoda joined us halfway through, windburned from a council trip. He greeted Katara with quiet affection that made her suddenly look younger. Not childish. Just somebody’s daughter.

I had not seen that version of her before.

It felt intimate in a way kissing had not prepared me for.

We ate sea-prune stew, roasted roots for Aang, fish for everyone who wanted it, and a sweet frozen berry dish Toph complained had “the texture of betrayal.”

Conversation moved around me like water.

Old names. Cousins. Repairs. Harbor politics. Sokka’s latest engineering problem. Who had married whom. Who had fallen through ice and blamed a seal.

I understood half of it.

Nobody stopped every thirty seconds to explain.

I liked that.

Belonging did not require becoming the center of someone else’s history.

After dinner, Katara asked if I wanted to walk.

Just us.

We followed a packed path beyond the newer buildings toward the shoreline.

The cold was enormous.

It had personality.

It entered my boots, found every gap in my coat, and appeared personally offended that I had bones.

Katara moved through it as if the wind were an old relative.

“Still want to walk?” she asked.

“I’m committed now.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

I looked at her.

She smiled.

I sighed. “Five more minutes.”

“Better.”

We stopped near a low ridge overlooking the water.

Katara looked back at the settlement.

“This used to be empty.”

I waited.

“Not empty empty. There were houses. But not… that.”

A crane turned slowly near the harbor.

“Do you hate it?”

“No.”

The answer came too quickly.

Katara heard it herself.

She pulled her hood tighter.

“Sometimes.”

That was more honest.

“I hated the North for a while,” she said. “Not the people. The way they looked at us like the South was a broken copy of them.”

I remembered stories of her first waterbending master refusing to teach women combat. Of customs she had challenged because tradition, to Katara, was never an excuse for injustice.

“Then I came home after the war and Northern builders were everywhere. New walls. New canals. New clothes. People kept saying progress.”

She scraped one boot through snow.

“And part of me wanted to scream that we had survived a hundred years. We didn’t need to become somebody else to prove we survived correctly.”

The wind tore at the words.

“What changed?” I asked.

“Nothing all at once.”

Very Katara answer.

She looked toward the harbor lights.

“I started asking who was choosing the changes. Whether local people had power. Whether new systems actually helped. Some did. Some didn’t.”

She smiled faintly.

“I learned nostalgia can protect things. It can also pretend the past was kinder than it was.”

I thought about Aang rebuilding festivals. Toph reading a letter from her father. Cranefish Town arguing about whether mixed neighborhoods were a corruption or a future.

“Home again,” I said.

Katara glanced at me.

“Apparently we have one theme.”

“Toph will hate that.”

“Good.”

We stood in silence.

Then Katara’s expression changed.

“What?” I asked.

She pointed.

Farther down the shore, a group of children had gathered around a cut in the ice. One was kneeling too close.

Katara was moving before I understood.

The ice broke.

A child disappeared.

Katara ran.

I followed badly.

Water exploded from the opening in a smooth column. The child rose inside it, coughing and terrified, carried toward Katara’s arms. She dropped to her knees, wrapped them in her own coat, and pressed glowing hands against their chest.

The other children screamed for adults.

I arrived breathless.

“Blankets,” Katara said.

I ran back toward the nearest house.

By the time Hakoda and half the neighborhood arrived, the child was conscious and furious about being carried.

Katara laughed with tears in her eyes.

Later, back at the house, she sat beside the fire in dry clothes while Gran Gran lectured everyone about shoreline safety as if Katara herself had fallen in.

Toph sat on the floor beside Katara’s chair, pretending her proximity meant nothing.

Aang brought tea.

I tucked a blanket over Katara’s knees.

She looked at me.

“This part hasn’t changed,” she said.

“What part?”

“Everybody knowing before you get home.”

From the kitchen, Sokka shouted, “The whole south knows!”

Katara groaned.

I laughed.

Outside, the transformed village kept building itself beneath old stars.

Katara’s home was not preserved in ice.

Neither was she.

Maybe loving where you came from meant allowing it to live long enough to become unfamiliar—and staying brave enough to keep asking whether the change still belonged to the people who called it home.

That night, Katara took me beyond the newest buildings to where the snow still swallowed sound.

She carried a waterskin at her hip but did not bend from it. Instead she knelt, pressed her palm to the ground, and drew a ribbon of snow upward until it melted between her fingers.

“This is the first place I taught myself,” she said.

I waited.

“Not this exact spot. Everything looks different.”

The confession was quieter than the wind.

She shaped the water into a small sphere, divided it into two, joined it again.

“I used to think coming home would feel like returning to something that had been waiting for me.”

“Did it?”

“Some parts.”

She looked toward the lights of the settlement. New roofs. Wider paths. Structures built with materials that had not been common here when she was a child.

“Other parts feel like arriving late to my own life.”

I moved closer but did not touch her until she reached for my hand.

“I’m happy they have more,” she said. “I wanted this. Food. healers. Trade. Choices. I just—”

“Miss what had to change for them to get it?”

Her fingers tightened around mine.

“Yes.”

There was no clever answer.

Aang would have understood loss shaped by absence. Toph would have understood home shaped by leaving. I understood only enough to stay beside her.

Katara bent the water into a thin arc and let it freeze into a clear bridge between two stones.

“Pretty,” I said.

“It won’t last.”

“Still pretty.”

She smiled.

By morning the bridge had softened at the edges.

By afternoon it was water again.

Nothing about that made it less real while it held.

Change had held.

So had we.
